title: Secrets Management and Least Privilege
oneLiner: Find the passwords and keys hiding in a repository, learn where secrets should live instead, then cut a service account's database rights down to exactly what its job needs.
keyTakeaway: Secrets never belong in source code, config files in Git, logs or URLs. Keep them in a secrets manager or the platform's secret store, or avoid them entirely with managed identities, and rotate any secret that leaks. Give every account only the permissions its job needs, so a stolen credential opens as little as possible.
explanation:
A secret is anything that grants access: passwords, API keys, connection strings, certificates' private keys, tokens. The most common way they leak is by being committed to a Git repository. Once pushed, a secret is copied to every clone, fork and build server, and it stays in the history even after a later commit deletes it. Automated bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Other leaks come from log lines that print tokens, keys in URLs (which end up in proxy and server logs), and passwords pasted into chat or tickets.

Secrets should be stored in a secrets manager, a service built to hold them, control and audit who reads them, and rotate them: Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes secrets, or the secret store of your CI/CD pipeline. For local development, .NET's user-secrets and an untracked .env file keep them out of the repository. Better still is no secret at all: managed identities and workload identity let the platform vouch for an app so it never holds a password. When a secret does leak, deleting it isn't enough; rotate it, meaning issue a new one and revoke the old.

Least privilege is the matching idea for permissions: every user, service and process gets the minimum access its job needs, and no more. The service that writes shift reports needs to read two tables and insert into a third, not db_owner on the whole database. When something is compromised, and eventually something is, the damage is limited to what that account could do. That limit is called the blast radius. The same applies to Windows services (a dedicated service account, not LocalSystem), people (separate admin accounts used only for admin work) and cloud roles.
